title: Short-Term Very High Carbohydrate Diet and Gut-Training Have Minor Effects on Gastrointestinal Status and Performance in Highly Trained Endurance Athletes
authors: King AJ, Etxebarria N, Ross ML, Garvican-Lewis L, Heikura IA, et al.
population: 19 elite male race walkers (26 km session) and 18 highly trained male and female distance runners (35 km run), MAX vs CON strategy
findings: MAX = 2 weeks high-CHO diet + gut-training, CHO loading and 90 g/h CHO during exercise; CON = lower ranges of current guidelines.
Race walkers: MAX associated with increased GI symptoms in the second half of exercise, especially upper GI (p < 0.01); no significant difference in breath H2 across exercise.
Runners: no major differences in I-FABP or GI symptoms between groups despite a 3-fold increase in exercise CHO intake in MAX.

Both groups improved similarly from pre to post intervention (CON 39 s; MAX 36 s; p = 0.002), suggesting higher CHO availability above current guidelines gives no additional advantage; considerable inter-individual variability.
Authors conclude athletes should meet minimum CHO guidelines, noting that with practice increased CHO intake can be tolerated and may contribute to performance outcomes.
limitations: Non-ultra distances (26-35 km); small groups; confounded by body-mass loss in several athletes and large aerobic gains from intensified training that may have masked small differences (stated by authors).
implications: Do not promise that 90+ g/h improves performance; present it as 'tolerance can be trained'.
Require meeting minimum CHO guidelines first; treat > 90 g/h as an athlete-chosen experiment with GI monitoring and fall-back to the previous tolerated rate.

verification.notes: Crossref match; findings confirmed against the Europe PMC abstract. Removed the unsupported 'non-blinded' limitation; clarified that the similar improvement refers to the runner cohort.
